Le nom de Sergius, auquel sont adressés quelques traités du Philosophe Chrétien, donne lieu à des remarques analogues; car il n'existe pas dans tous les manuscrits.

11° Le manuscrit 2325 ne renferme pas les poètes; ceux-ci devaient donc former à l'origine une collection à part.

12° Le manuscrit 2325 ne renferme aucun traité de vieil auteur important, qui ne soit dans le manuscrit de Saint-Marc.

Il contient en moins le traité d'Ostanès, les chapitres de Zosime à Théodore, le serment de Pappus, le traité de Cléopâtre (poids et mesures) et quelques autres articles; articles qui manquent également dans le manuscrit 2327.

La liste des signes offre certaines confusions et diversités (v. pages 97 et 98 du présent volume).

Le manuscrit 2325 ne contient aucune trace des traités de Comarius.

Il contient en plus, par rapport à Saint-Marc, certains traités techniques, tel que celui de l'arabe Salmanas sur les perles, et la fabrication des émeraudes et autres pierres colorées, d'après le livre du Sanctuaire. La Chrysopée de Cosmas est ajoutée à la suite, d'une écriture plus moderne et presque effacée.

Dans le manuscrit 2325, l'ordre relatif est absolument, et du commencement à la fin, le même que celui du manuscrit 2327. Ce dernier dérive évidemment d'un type commun, mais complété par des intercalations et additions considérables.

Au contraire, l'ordre relatif est très différent entre ces deux manuscrits et le manuscrit de Saint-Marc : on y reviendra.

13° Examinons les traités qui manquent dans le manuscrit de Saint-Marc et qui existent dans le manuscrit 2327. Parlons d'abord de ceux qui portent des noms d'auteurs.

Le manuscrit 2327 débute par la lettre de Psellus adressée à Xiphilin. Dans certains manuscrits, cette lettre est adressée à Michel Cérularius; l'identité complète des deux lettres aurait besoin d'être vérifiée.

Le traité de Comarius se trouve dans le manuscrit 2327, sous sa forme la plus complète.

Je signalerai encore :

Le traité de Jean l'archiprêtre, qui manque dans le 2325;

Le traité de Salmanas et celui des émeraudes, qui s'y trouvent au contraire, ainsi que la Chrysopée de Cosmas, transcrite à la suite et à une époque postérieure dans le 2325;

Les livres de Sophé (Chéops);

La lettre d'Isis à Horus;

Le livre de Démocrite à Leucippe;

Le traité d'Agathodémon sur l'oracle d'Orphée;

La coction excellente de l'or, avec les procédés de Jamblique;

La chimie domestique de Moïse;

14° Enfin, parmi les articles anonymes manquant dans le manuscrit de Saint-Marc, et existant dans le manuscrit 2327, on peut citer :

La liste des faiseurs d'or (manquant dans le 2325).

The name of Sergius, to whom some treatises of the Christian Philosopher are addressed, calls for similar remarks, since it does not appear in all the manuscripts.

11° Manuscript 2325 does not contain the poets; these must therefore originally have formed a separate collection.

12° Manuscript 2325 contains no treatise by an important early author that is not also in the Saint Mark manuscript. <note>The Saint Mark manuscript is the famous codex Marcianus in the Library of Saint Mark in Venice, the oldest and most important manuscript of the Greek alchemists.</note>

It lacks the treatise of Ostanes, the chapters of Zosimos to Theodore, the oath of Pappus, the treatise of Cleopatra (weights and measures) and a few other articles; these articles are likewise missing from manuscript 2327.

The list of signs shows certain confusions and variations (see pages 97 and 98 of the present volume).

Manuscript 2325 contains no trace of the treatises of Comarius.

Compared with Saint Mark, it contains in addition certain technical treatises, such as that of the Arab Salmanas on pearls, and the making of emeralds and other colored stones, according to the Book of the Sanctuary. The <term>Chrysopoeia</term> <gloss>art of making gold</gloss> of Cosmas is added afterward, in a more modern and almost faded hand.

In manuscript 2325, the relative order is exactly the same as that of manuscript 2327, from beginning to end. The latter clearly derives from a common type, but one completed by considerable insertions and additions.

By contrast, the relative order differs greatly between these two manuscripts and the Saint Mark manuscript: we will return to this.

13° Let us examine the treatises that are missing from the Saint Mark manuscript but present in manuscript 2327. First, let us discuss those that bear authors' names.

Manuscript 2327 opens with the letter of Psellus addressed to Xiphilinus. <note>Michael Psellus (11th century) was a leading Byzantine scholar; John Xiphilinus was his contemporary and later Patriarch of Constantinople.</note> In some manuscripts, this letter is addressed to Michael Cerularius; whether the two letters are wholly identical would need to be verified.

The treatise of Comarius is found in manuscript 2327 in its most complete form.

I will also point out:

The treatise of John the Archpriest, which is missing from 2325;

The treatise of Salmanas and that on emeralds, which on the contrary are found there, as is the Chrysopoeia of Cosmas, copied afterward and at a later period in 2325;

The books of Sophe (Cheops); <note>Sophe is a Greek form of the name of the pharaoh Khufu, known to the Greeks as Cheops.</note>

The letter of Isis to Horus;

The book of Democritus to Leucippus;

The treatise of Agathodaimon on the oracle of Orpheus;

The excellent cooking of gold, with the procedures of Iamblichus;

The domestic chemistry of Moses;

14° Finally, among the anonymous articles missing from the Saint Mark manuscript and present in manuscript 2327, one may cite:

The list of the gold-makers (missing from 2325).

Ray 4) fait aussi mention du Subbuteo et du Dendrofalco comme de deux espèces distinctes. Frisch 5) en donnant une bonne figure de l'adulte du hobereau, lui attribue très mal à propos les noms de Rochier, Lithofalco ou Esalon. Brisson 6) a le premier réuni au hobereau le Falco arborealis d'Albert le grand ou le Dendrofalco de Gessner, mais il emploie ce dernier nom pour désigner l'espèce. Linné 7), ayant suivi cet exemple, préfère cependant le nom de Falco subbuteo à celui de Dendrofalco, et à dater de cette époque, le hobereau figure dans tous les écrits des naturalistes, sous la dénomination latine de Falco subbuteo. Il existe, dans les différents ouvrages d'histoire naturelle, un grand nombre de figures plus ou moins bonnes du hobereau; nous nous bornons à citer celles contenues dans les ouvrages de Buffon 8), de Borkhausen 9), de Naumann 10) et de Gould 11).

Le hobereau porte en anglais le nom de «hobby.» En Allemagne, il est assez généralement connu sous celui de Baumfalke; cependant, la plupart des naturalistes allemands modernes ont cru devoir suivre l'exemple de Naumann, qui a conféré à cette espèce le nom allemand de Lerchenfalke, ce qui signifie faucon aux alouettes. Les fauconniers hollandais se servent indistinctement, pour désigner le hobereau, des noms de «boomvalk» et de «molliet»; mais ce dernier mot est évidemment corrompu de «baillet», usité du temps de Merula 12).

Le hobereau a été observé dans presque toutes les parties tempérées de l'Europe; il habite aussi la grande Bretagne 13) et la Suède méridionale 14), mais il ne se trouve, ni en Islande, ni dans le nord de la Scandinavie. Il est commun en Hollande, en France et en Allemagne; les naturalistes italiens en font mention comme d'un oiseau généralement connu dans leur pays; Küster 15) l'énumère parmi les espèces de la Sardaigne, et le comte von der Mühle 16) constate qu'en Grèce il est commun en hiver, mais qu'en été il habite de préférence la Rumélie. Les voyageurs hollandais et Mr. Smith ont recueilli des individus de cette espèce au Cap de Bonne Espérance; Pallas dit qu'elle se trouve en abondance dans toute la Russie et la Sibérie jusqu'au Kamtschatka 17), et le musée britannique 18) en possède un individu originaire de la Chine 19). En été, le hobereau habite de préférence les petits bois, où il établit son aire sur les arbres élevés et près de leur cime. Les œufs, au nombre de trois à quatre, sont d'un blanc sale, recouvert de tous côtés par des taches de forme assez diverse, plus ou moins distinctes ou lavées, et d'un brun rougeâtre. Il quitte, en hiver, les contrées froides et tempérées de l'Europe, et c'est alors qu'il fait de

préférence la chasse aux alouettes qu'il a l'habitude d'accompagner lors de leurs migrations. Il se nourrit également d'autres oiseaux de petite taille, particulièrement d'hirondelles, et on le voit souvent poursuivre ou prendre toutes sortes d'insectes, soit à défaut d'autre nourriture, soit par prédilection pour ce genre de chasse, soit lorsqu'au jeune âge il n'a pas encore acquis assez de dextérité pour attraper les oiseaux qui forment sa proie favorite.

Le hobereau est le plus doux et le plus familier des oiseaux de proie d'Europe; il s'apprivoise facilement, surtout quand il a été enlevé du nid, et son éducation ainsi que son affaitage ne demandent que peu de soins. Excellent voleur, cette qualité et celles que nous venons d'énumérer le rendraient très précieux pour la chasse au vol, s'il était doué d'un caractère plus féroce et plus sanguinaire, et s'il savait se servir avec plus de dextérité de ses serres. Réduit en captivité, où il ne peut exercer ses forces comme à l'état sauvage, on ne parvient pas même à lui faire voler des alouettes qu'il sait cependant fort bien attraper, lorsqu'il se trouve en pleine liberté; aussi arrive-t-il souvent qu'au lieu de poursuivre le gibier, il s'amuse à faire la chasse aux hannetons, aux sauterelles ou à d'autres insectes qu'il rencontre dans les airs. Il paraît cependant que d'autres peuples en font encore usage: car Pallas 20) constate que les Calmouks se servent de cette espèce comme oiseau de chasse, et on voit par une notice publiée récemment par Mr. Drummond Hay 21), que ce petit faucon est fort en honneur chez l'Empereur de Maroc. to determine the species, because Aristotle neglected to provide a description of it <note>1)</note>. Aldrovandi <note>2)</note> follows the example of Belon by describing and illustrating the hobby under the name <term>Subbuteo</term>, which does not prevent him from later enumerating <note>3)</note>, as a distinct species, the <term>Falco arborealis</term> of Albertus Magnus. Ray <note>4)</note> also mentions the <term>Subbuteo</term> and the <term>Dendrofalco</term> as two distinct species. Frisch <note>5)</note>, while providing a good illustration of the adult hobby, very inappropriately attributes to it the names <term>Rochier</term>, <term>Lithofalco</term>, or <term>Esalon</term>. Brisson <note>6)</note> was the first to reunite the <term>Falco arborealis</term> of Albertus Magnus (or the <term>Dendrofalco</term> of Gessner) with the hobby, but he uses the latter name to designate the species. Linnaeus <note>7)</note>, having followed this example, nevertheless prefers the name <term>Falco subbuteo</term> to that of <term>Dendrofalco</term>, and from that time, the hobby has appeared in all the writings of naturalists under the Latin designation <term>Falco subbuteo</term>. There exists, in various natural history works, a large number of more or less accurate illustrations of the hobby; we shall limit ourselves to citing those contained in the works of Buffon <note>8)</note>, Borkhausen <note>9)</note>, Naumann <note>10)</note>, and Gould <note>11)</note>.

The hobby bears the name "hobby" in English. In Germany, it is quite generally known by the name <term>Baumfalke</term> <gloss>tree falcon</gloss>; however, most modern German naturalists have thought it necessary to follow the example of Naumann, who conferred upon this species the German name <term>Lerchenfalke</term> <gloss>lark falcon</gloss>. Dutch falconers use the names "boomvalk" and "molliet" indiscriminately to designate the hobby; but the latter word is clearly a corruption of "baillet," used in the time of Merula <note>12)</note>.

The hobby has been observed in almost all the temperate parts of Europe; it also inhabits Great Britain <note>13)</note> and southern Sweden <note>14)</note>, but it is found neither in Iceland nor in northern Scandinavia. It is common in Holland, France, and Germany; Italian naturalists mention it as a bird generally known in their country; Küster <note>15)</note> enumerates it among the species of Sardinia, and Count von der Mühle <note>16)</note> notes that in Greece it is common in winter, but that in summer it prefers to inhabit Rumelia. Dutch travelers and Mr. Smith have collected individuals of this species at the Cape of Good Hope; Pallas says that it is found in abundance throughout Russia and Siberia as far as Kamchatka <note>17)</note>, and the British Museum <note>18)</note> possesses an individual originating from China <note>19)</note>. In summer, the hobby prefers to inhabit small woods, where it builds its nest on high trees, near their tops. The eggs, numbering three to four, are of a dirty white, covered on all sides with spots of rather diverse shapes, more or less distinct or washed, and of a reddish-brown color. In winter, it leaves the cold and temperate regions of Europe, and it is then that it makes 

<column-break/>

a point of hunting larks, which it has the habit of accompanying during their migrations. It also feeds on other small-sized birds, particularly swallows, and one often sees it pursuing or catching all sorts of insects, either for lack of other food, by preference for this type of hunting, or when, at a young age, it has not yet acquired enough dexterity to catch the birds that form its favorite prey.

The hobby is the gentlest and most familiar of the birds of prey of Europe; it is easily tamed, especially when taken from the nest, and its training and manning require little care. An excellent flyer, this quality and those we have just enumerated would make it very precious for falconry, if it were gifted with a more ferocious and bloodthirsty character, and if it knew how to use its talons with more dexterity. Reduced to captivity, where it cannot exercise its strength as in the wild state, one does not even succeed in making it hunt larks, which it knows how to catch very well, however, when it is in full liberty; thus it often happens that instead of pursuing game, it amuses itself by hunting cockchafers, grasshoppers, or other insects that it encounters in the air. Not being able to be used with success except for the flight of birds using a lure or by "escape" <note>a method where the hawk is flown at wild quarry without prior conditioning</note>, this falcon is not in the least esteemed today, and it is never seen among falconers. It appears, however, that other peoples still make use of it: for Pallas <note>20)</note> notes that the Kalmyks use this species as a hunting bird, and we see by a notice published recently by Mr. Drummond Hay <note>21)</note>, that this small falcon is held in high honor by the Emperor of Morocco. Although the old falconers thought little of the hobby as a hunting bird <note>22)</note>, and often only mentioned it in passing, this falcon has nonetheless acquired a certain celebrity, because it was the bird chosen by preference by youth <note>23)</note>, by bird-catchers <note>24)</note>, and in general by people whose rank and means did not allow them to maintain falconries; from this comes, probably, the usage that exists in some provinces of France to give the name <term>hobereau</term> to minor lords or country gentlemen who treat hunting as a matter of profit rather than pleasure <note>25)</note>.

THE ELEONORA'S FALCON. <note>Original: "LE FAUCON SAPHIR"</note> — There exists in Syria, Greece, Sardinia, and probably also in several other parts of southern Europe, a falcon resembling the hobby in its wings, which extend beyond the tail, but which is of a larger size, and whose plumage offers a brown, uniform, and dark tint in adults, lighter in the young. This falcon, discovered only a few years ago and described by Professor Gené <note>26)</note> of Turin as a new species under the name <term>Falco Eleonorae</term>, was not unknown to the ancient falconers.

Het huis te *Heemskerk* heeft men u genoemd te vóren,
Of anderſints het huis te *Zevenbergen*, maar
Toen ’t oud en ridderlyk geſlagt van Heemſkerk waar
Het lévens ligt ontroofd, vervierd gy aan Vianen,
Van die aan Arenberg, om dus het ſpoor te bânen
Waar door heer de Hartaln u heeft voor geld gekogt,
En u den nieuwen naam *Marquette* toe gebragt,
Naar ’t dorp *Marquette*, in ’t land van Vlaanderen gelégen.
Dus hebt gy ménigmaal een and’ren heer gekrégen,
Eêr *Rendorp* u heeft tot zyn eigendom gemaakt,
*Marquette* hoe veel zoet en zuur hebt gy geſmaakt,

<column-break/>

Van uwen opbouw, nu vyf eeuwen haaſt geléden?
Wat heeft men ménigmaal rondom uw grond geſtrédên?
Dat gras, en bloem en kruid ſcheen enkel bloed te zyn;
Maar na die ſtormen kreegt ge een lieven zonnenſchyn
Van eendragt en vermaak, gelyk we u nu aanſchouwen,
Daar gy het oog kunt in verwond'ring bezig houwen.
Als men uw Voorpoort langs de Heinigen ontmoet,
By ’t ſchaduwend geboomt, ’t geen Febus held'ren gloed
Een weinig mátigd, om hier meêr vermaak te vinden.
*Marquette* ’k zou me altoos aan uw gezigt verbindên,
Tenzv my de Amſtel-ſtad weêr dwong te rug te gaan,
Dewyl myn zangeres haar wand’ling heeft voldaan.
Lang moet ge, ô ad’lyk huis! uw Torentje verheffen!
Nooit moet u tegenſpoed, of ramp, of onheil treffen!
Maar ſtreke tot *Rendorps* vreugde, als hy de buiten lugt
Komt zoeken op uw grond, om daar de zoete vrugt
Der lieff'lyke eenzaamheid met vrolykheid te ontvangen,
Zo ſtrekt uw beider Naam het ſlot van myne zangen.
ô Kenn'merland wat zyt gy aan ’t geval verpligt,
Daar zo veel landſieraad is op uw grond geſtigt
Van Dorpen, Sloten, en beroemde Hérenhoven;
Het ſchvnt ge Italiën zyn luiſter wilt beróven
Met uwe uitmuntende ſierâden, ſchoon- en pragt,
Natuur heeft, zo het ſchynt, hier alleſt-zaam gebragt
Waf haar vermogen ooit een landſtreeck heeft gegevên,
Zy heeft ’t beleid en kunſt ook herwaards aangedréven,
Om zig te páren met haar toegenégenheid,
Die zo veel wond’ren heeft op uwen grond verſpreid.
Herulers koft ge u nu eens uit graf verheffen,
Met wat verwondering zou Kenn’merland u treffen?
Uwe oude woonſteê zou voor u onkenny'lyk zyn,
De digte boſſchen, die den held’ren zonnenſchyn
Wel eer beletten om het aardryk te genâken,
Zyn nu geheel verſtrooid, verwoeſt, om plaats máken
Voor Huizen, Tuinen, en voor Dorpen groots van ſtand,
Toen de Arendſlandaard wierd op uwen grond geplant
Door Romens legermagt, toen laagt gy haaſt begrâven
In diepe onwétênheid, men wiſt van land, nog haven,
Men kende ſtreeck nog weg, maar wel een woesten grond,
En náre boſſen, daar ge u zelven onderwond
De Goden van dit land met ’t offer te veréren,
Zo weet natuur en tyd het alles om te kéren.
Vaar wel dan Kenn'merland! vergroot van dag tot dag
In ſchoonheid en ſieraad! wyl ik met diep ontzag
Van uwe gronden ga, om elders weêr te vinden
’t Geen ik in u verlaat, ſchoon gy my ſchynt te binden
Aan ’t geen ik heb gezien, en in myn weg ontmoet.
De hemel géve aan u zyn heil en overvloed,
Om uwe Héren, en bewoonders te behágen!
Myn Digt-nimf moet zig naar de Tekenkunſt gedrágen
Daar zy haar bénen leid daar volgt zy op het ſpoor.
Wel aan, Terpſichoré! ga dan vryhartig voor,
Ik zal myn zangeres ſteeds aan uwe Etsnaald páren,
Geen Eendragt kan meêr vreugde, of gróter welluſt báren,
Dan daar de Tekenkunſt paard met de Poëzy,
Die beide hunnen troon beveſtigen aan ’t Y.
Hier zwygt myn zangſter om den adem te herhalen,
Tot dat zy ’t landvermaak op nieuw weêr af komt málen,
En met een nieuwen luſt een nieuwe reis begint,
Wyl zy van Kenn’merland zig thans voldaan bevind.

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous account of the estates of Meervliet and Velzen, the poetic journey continues through the landscapes and country houses of Merestyn, Haringkarspel, Adrichem, Heemskerk, and finally, Marquette.</meta>

To greet you anew, now that the Winter has departed,
Speak, speak old *Merestyn*, for it has become evident to you,
That *Haringkarspel* leaves you, and finds again,
As the fresh scent of Astraea binds Boreas's cold,
And locks up the winter frost, and causes the days to grow,
To make Flora and Pomona <note>Goddesses of flowers and fruit, respectively.</note> bloom with their gifts.
Old *Merestyn*, formerly called the *Wyckerschans* <note>Literal meaning: "Wijk rampart/defense work."</note>,
Your *Haringkarspel* makes your name famous everywhere,
And gives you more luster than all your gracefulness.
Farewell old *Merestyn*! I must tread further again,
Where noble *Adrichem* invites me with its beauty.
Oh praiseworthy landscape! Your glory is too great
For my meager song to give you your due fame:
Antiquity once described you with the name of *Arkum*,
When you mirrored yourself in the bright Swan-lake,
Which has now dried up, in order to show you a new
Delight in its greenery, in place of its water.
It seems that all the ornament wishes to crown you alike,
Where you thrust your proud gable-splendor and tower
High at Sint Aagte-dyk, freed from the war-steel
Of the small Frisians, which you once had to feel,
When the war, to cool its courage on your Castle,
Destroyed, ruined, and demolished it to the ground,
And heaped the former ornament in ruins together,
From which Lord vander Burg has reborn you again,
And placed you in a better state than ever before,
Just as we, oh *Adrichem*! now see in your condition,
And discover your ornament from afar along your broad Lane,
Planted on both sides with high trees.
Oh beautiful sight! You can awaken my heart to joy,
The more so, when I think of who often enjoys rest here,
The alert *Trip* <note>A prominent Amsterdam patrician family known for their wealth and political involvement.</note>, who hears the *Y* and the *Amstel*
Being brought to the jurisdiction of Themis's laws <note>Themis is the Greek goddess of divine law and order.</note> and her tribunal,
Has chosen this old noble House for his pleasure.
What salvation, oh *Adrichem*! do you enjoy through your Lord,
When he lays his care down upon your ground,
To find a little rest there, unconcerned?
To which he feels himself bound by the office of Alderman,
To close off evil through the cut of the lawful sword.
Even though our Amsterdam is renowned throughout the Universe,
By power and commerce, by thousands of ships,
Which carry the finest of the East and the West on our Y-stream,
It still needs greater fame, since justice with wise policy
Is constantly maintained there, in order to punish
Evil with caution, and to reward the good.
Oh noble *Trip*! That praise must crown you first,
To which you constantly devote your care, and diligence, and time,
When you step onto our Capitol at the marble Tribunal,
To weigh lawful justice with Astraea's scales <note>Astraea is the goddess of justice.</note>,
May heaven give you its salvation and favor and blessing!
And keep your *Adrichem* in the same state with you!
While my Songstress leaves this landscape,
To behold the stately *Merestyn* by the shading green.
Has one of the Gods founded this ornament of country buildings
For his pleasure? Oh Yes! I do not doubt,
Whether Faunus <note>Roman god of the forest, plains, and fields.</note> holds supreme rule here,
Since the care for the Land has been given to him by fate.
Oh Faunus! I then approach your green walking-paths,

<column-break/>

But with the reverence that befits your greatness.
My Songstress shall, joyous and doubly satisfied,
If you deign to hear her lowly Song,
Depart from here, for nothing can charm her more,
Than to proclaim your praise and glory everywhere,
And *spell* <note>In Dutch, "spelt" can mean "spells out" or "articulates." The text plays on the surname "Vander Spelt."</note> Faunus's great name in her Songs.
But Echo, what do you wish to make known to me?
Why have you driven the Name of *Spelt* to me again?
What can, what shall I understand from this single word?
Speak Echo! Speak on now! But alas! What ails me,
That I ask of you the speech that has long since vanished,
From the time that Narcissus made you weep for his unrequited love?
Have you vanished into air, and do you keep only the reverberation,
How then do I become aware of the word *Spelt* through you?
How do I find this secret, or what it wishes to show?
Am I deceived? How! Would Faunus not live here?
Oh No! For *Merestyn* belongs to Lord *vander Spelt*.
Oh Echo! You have presented the truth to me,
Though like the Sphinx formerly let his riddles be heard.
Oh airy *Merestyn*! You can charm the eye
Through your perfect state, and neatly planted lane;
How far can the lush eye safely pasture here,
To obtain all the land- and court-pleasures at once,
In the shadow of the high-topped trees:
Your neat square building caused my doubting,
When I first received your beautiful sight,
Which made me conclude that one of the Gods
Had fled the hall of Jove <note>Jupiter.</note> for your pleasure,
To find his delight here in solitude,
But no, Lord *vander Spelt* finds his joy and rest here,
When the flowering season makes tree, and herb, and flower bloom.
Oh *Merestyn*! You must always grow in esteem,
So that your luster increases even more day by day,
Farewell! Since *Heemskerk* invites me with its beauty,
Therefore I step forward to amuse myself there further.
Old and graceful Village! You make my zeal blaze,
When I see your neat building of Church and Tower,
My attention is enraptured and absorbed, who
Does not also marvel, who beholds you, after so many years,
In such a state? Preserved from the dangers
Of domestic discord, whose bloody war-glow
Has destroyed, ruined, and turned so many Cities
Into a heap of ruins in mad arrogance,
Who counts the Villages and Castles together,
That she has cast down! When the raging war-sword
Of the Hook and Cod factions everywhere sullied the fertile earth
With the blood of miserable subjects,
Which often made orphans and widows melt in their tears.
Happy *Heemskerk*! That you are still preserved,
As the state shows, in which one greets you,
To sing your praise also with my Songstress.
The Second William <note>William II, Count of Holland.</note> could force the power of the Frisians here,
Through the built-up Castle, for your safety,
Thus one turns away an enemy through wisdom and policy,
To save the subjects from his rage,
Resistance alone makes his vengeful courage subside,
When he threatens everything with fire and steel and cord.
Inhuman war, what people you have murdered,
And ruined field and land, and ravaged them,
For all horrors are bound together with you:
Here the Farmer is chased from his hut and stable,
There the child is un-souled, yonder one violates a chaste Virgin,

<meta>catchword: En</meta>

---

And sets house and home ablaze with the war-torch:
One sees the withering old age wandering along the lands,
Plundered and chased, stripped of property,
The infant is killed in its mother’s arms.
But how! What urges me to paint those horrors?
Your antiquity, *Heemskerk*, made me wander from the path,
Thus I turn again anew to your land-ornament.
How joyfully you stroke the eye, when one goes playing
Along this road, which the trees give shadow,
Let Tiberius live in his lust
On the wanton Caprea, I choose your humility,
Where virtue joins itself, which spreads a more beautiful luster
Than any luxurious court can show to the eye,
Farewell, *Marquette* must in the end crown my song
With its widely famous and ancient foundation,
Which King Willem, Count of Holland, has erected,
Just as my Muse just sang by *Heemskerk*,
Whereby the wild Frisian was tamed and subdued
In his wantonness: We still see the remnant
Of the strength in the old Roundel, although the noble castle
Is destroyed and ruined by stinging war-flags;
The Kennemerlander thus seemed to gnaw even his own heart,
To smother Heemstede, Brederode, and Assendelft in their fall
Under the rubble of this demolished rampart.
Oh blind revenge! What horrors can you provide!
*Marquette* felt the suffering that Haarlem had committed,
That noble castle suffered for your fierce rage and hatred:
One judges its strength and firmly built state,
When Duke Albrecht with his gathered servants,
Had to besiege the noble castle here for eleven weeks,
Before the Lord of Heemskerk bowed to his war-power,
But Haarlem! Although you brought this house to a fall,
What did you accomplish, other than to have its proud gable
Lift itself high again with new luster,
Out of the overturned rubble, and out of the dreadful... <note>The text "Juiſter" appears to be an archaic or corrupted term for gloom or sorrow.</note>
You have not hit the mark at all, although the bow
Of your fury was drawn to the most intense degree,
To overcome everything by violence and rage:
But strong and old Roundel, is it truth, what they say,
Stood in your center-round a Tower erected,
Which could serve as a beacon to the sailors,
To discover their right course at night, through the burning light?
But how! You do not answer, and feed my doubting,
I leave that uncertain matter then as I received it,
To trace the origin of your Name, *Marquette*:
The house at *Heemskerk* you were called before,
Or otherwise the house at *Zevenbergen*, but
When the old and knightly lineage of Heemskerk was
Deprived of the light of life, you passed to Vianen,
From there to Arenberg, to thus clear the path
Through which Lord de Hartaln bought you for money,
And brought the new name *Marquette* to you,
According to the village *Marquette*, situated in the land of Flanders.
Thus you have many times received a different lord,
Before *Rendorp* made you his property,
*Marquette*, how much sweet and sour have you tasted,

<column-break/>

Since your construction, now almost five centuries ago?
What has one many times fought for around your ground?
That grass, and flower, and herb seemed to be only blood;
But after those storms you received a lovely sunshine
Of concord and pleasure, just as we see you now,
Where you can keep the eye busy in wonder.
When one meets your Foregate along the Heinigen,
By the shadowing trees, which moderate Phoebus's <note>The sun's.</note> bright glow
A little, in order to find more pleasure here.
*Marquette* I would always bind myself to your sight,
Unless the Amstel-city forced me to go back,
Since my songstress has completed her wandering.
Long must you, oh noble house! lift your small Tower!
Never must adversity, or disaster, or misfortune meet you!
But stretch to *Rendorp's* joy, when he comes to seek
The outside air on your ground, to receive there the sweet fruit
Of lovely solitude with cheerfulness,
Thus your both Names stretch the end of my songs.
Oh Kennemerland what are you obligated to the event,
Where so many land-ornaments have been founded on your ground
Of Villages, Castles, and famous Noble-courts;
It seems you wish to rob Italy of its luster
With your excellent ornaments, beauty, and splendor,
Nature has, it seems, brought everything here
That her power has ever given to a region,
She has also driven the policy and art hitherward,
To pair itself with her affection,
Which has spread so many wonders upon your ground.
If you could now lift yourself once from the grave,
With what wonder would Kennemerland strike you?
Your old dwelling-place would be unrecognizable to you,
The dense forests, which formerly prevented the bright sunshine
From approaching the earth,
Are now entirely scattered, destroyed, to make room
For Houses, Gardens, and for Villages of great state,
When the Eagle-standard was planted on your ground
By Rome's military force, then you lay almost buried
In deep ignorance, one knew of neither land nor harbor,
One knew neither region nor path, but a wild ground,
And gloomy forests, where you undertook yourself
To honor the Gods of this land with the sacrifice,
Thus nature and time know how to turn everything.
Farewell then Kennemerland! Grow from day to day
In beauty and ornament! While I go with deep awe
From your grounds, to find elsewhere again
What I leave in you, although you seem to bind me
To what I have seen, and met on my way.
May heaven give you its salvation and abundance,
To please your Lords, and inhabitants!
My Poem-nymph must conduct herself toward the Art of Drawing
Where she leads her legs, there she follows on the trail.
Well then, Terpsichore! <note>The muse of dance and chorus.</note> Go then freely ahead,
I shall constantly pair my songstress to your Etching-needle,
No Concord can bear more joy, or greater delight,
Than where the Art of Drawing pairs with Poetry,
Which both confirm their throne at the Y.
Here my songstress is silent to catch her breath,
Until she comes to paint the land-pleasure again anew,
And with a new lust begins a new journey,
Since she finds herself satisfied with Kennemerland for now.

-> G. TYSENS. <-
